item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of October 26 - November 02, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending November 02, 2026

The best design isn’t always the one that covers the space most evenly. This week’s papers keep asking a more practical question: what uncertainty are we trying to reduce, and what assumptions are we willing to trust? That’s a useful shift for anyone designing experiments where runs are costly, measurements are clustered, or the system keeps changing under our feet.

The most immediately portable idea comes from Karl et al.’s sphericity filter for nondeterministic experiments. It starts with a familiar goal—choose a space-filling design—but also protects precision for effects we think may matter. Across their examples, that small change often bought better prediction precision at modest geometric cost. In a constrained lipid-nanoparticle study, efficiency improved 27.5% over a geometry-focused comparator, with a 2.3% increase in median geometric cost. The catch is important: the filter needs a working model to say which effects to protect. In the same study, a raw coefficient-based filter actually reduced efficiency. So this is a promising way to refine a candidate design, not a license to treat the model as unquestionable.

Cao et al. offer a quieter but equally practical reminder from oat trials: plants from the same plot are not independent experimental units. Their Bayesian ordinal model accounts for ordered growth stages and plot-level clustering, then compares models by holding out whole plots. Leaving out the plot effect substantially hurt prediction and made some contrast intervals look narrower than they should. By contrast, adding a spatial field provided little detectable benefit on these layouts. For quality engineers, the lesson travels well: model the randomization and sampling structure first; add spatial complexity when the data can support it.

Zanotta et al.’s FIDE takes design selection into less familiar territory: measurements of evolving population laws, where aggregate observations can’t identify the full state. FIDE first enforces a scientific-risk allowance, then prefers designs that require a smaller correction to a frozen reference dynamics. That preference improved held-out action measures in several simulations, including a 32-dimensional example. But it is explicitly reference-dependent: when the baseline was misspecified, its downstream advantage could reverse. Think of it as a way to choose among designs given a trusted reference, not as protection against a bad one.

And then there’s Moradi et al., who put experimental design on one athlete’s training schedule. EPICOACH proposes feasible workouts that balance learning about the rider with improving performance, while recording predictions before the rides—an appealing discipline for any adaptive system. The results are a good reality check: heart-rate forecasts improved over several baselines, but segment-time forecasts did not, and early climb forecasts missed the athlete’s improvement. Safety checks also vetoed the top-ranked overload plan in both live cycles. That’s not a failure of the idea; it’s a reminder that a clever experiment planner still needs a model that can keep up with a changing process.

Across the week, the common thread is design for the decision you actually care about—and make your assumptions visible. Which assumption in your own experiment would you most want to stress-test before trusting the design?

Featured Papers This Week

  • Moradi et al.: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables (DOE)
  • Zanotta et al.: FIDE: Fiber-Informed Differentiable Experimental Design for Reference-Relative Law Dynamics (DOE)
  • Cao et al.: Bayesian Ordinal Analysis of Cereal Growth Stage Data from Oat Trials in Western Australia (DOE)
  • Karl et al.: A Sphericity Filter for Space-Filling Designs in Nondeterministic Experiments (DOE)
